### anchorAtGrip {#anchoratgrip}

Whether a held object pivots about the grip rather than about its own centre of mass.

Lean on a rod and the table pushes back at its tip. Left alone the rod turns about its
centre of mass halfway down the shaft, so the far end going one way sends the grip end the
other, and the hand with it. Press a stick into a table in life and it does not drive your
hand into your elbow: the arm is the anchor and the stick pivots about the hand. Moving the
centre of mass onto the grip says that in the only language the solver reads.

```csharp
public bool anchorAtGrip
```

### correctionGain {#correctiongain}

How much of the object's remaining offset from the grip the hold removes in a single step. 1
removes all of it, which is exact while nothing interferes and a per-step reversal the moment
anything does: a contact pushes the object, the write puts it straight back, and that alternation
is what jitter is. Lower values settle over several steps. Smooth motion costs nothing either
way, because the grip's own velocity is fed forward separately and only the error is damped.

0.25 is the measured knee. Higher and every contact case is worse; lower and smooth
carrying starts to lag. Between 1.0 and 0.25 the smooth cases do not move at all, so the
damping is bought for nothing.

```csharp
[Range(0.05, 1)]
public float correctionGain
```

**Returns** [`float`](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.single)

[View source](https://git.cie-group.cz/vr-framework/vrf4/core/-/blob/interaction/physics-hold/Runtime/Scripts/Interaction/PhysicsHold.cs#L231)

### ignoreAllHands {#ignoreallhands}

Whether the object also stops colliding with the player's other hands, not only the one holding
it. On, and it is a deliberate departure from what real hands would do: measured, a free hand
brushing a held prop pushes it 28 mm out of the grip, and because the hold writes the pose back
the two alternate every step, which is jitter. Hand tracking gives no touch feedback, so the
player cannot feel their own hand about to do this and reads the result as a fault.

```csharp
public bool ignoreAllHands
```

### maxAcceleration {#maxacceleration}

How fast the hold may change the object's velocity, in metres per second squared. The strength
of the hold: bounding the change per step is what stops a written velocity behaving like an
infinitely strong hand, and what keeps a hand entering a pile of props from firing them across
the room.

Bracketed on both sides. Below about 250 the hold cannot keep up with its own palm; at 800
and above it starts cancelling contact impulses outright, and a held object stops losing
arguments with walls.

```csharp
[Header("Velocity mode")]
public float maxAcceleration
```

### maxGripTwist {#maxgriptwist}

How far the object may turn the hand away from where the player is holding it, in degrees,
before the grip gives and the object turns inside it instead. Past the angle the excess is
handed back by re-recording the grip; inside it the grip is rigid, which is what makes turning
your wrist turn what you are holding.

**Zero, which is off, and it should stay off.** The framework's rule is that a hand does
not move or turn against what it is holding in any circumstance. A grip that gives has to
decide when, and it reads as the object wandering during ordinary handling. Use
[`turnsTheHand`](/api/vrframework-interaction-runtime/HoldSettings#turnsthehand) for the case this was reached for.

```csharp
public float maxGripTwist
```

**Returns** [`float`](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.single)

### maxOffset {#maxoffset}

How far the hold will stretch before it stops trying any harder, in metres.

Without it, an object pressed into a wall is asked for a velocity that grows for as long as
the player keeps pushing, and a heavy one is driven clean through. Bounding it turns "as
hard as it takes" into a strongest push, which is what a hand is: the object stops where
the world stops it, and how far the tracked hand has gone past that is break distance's
business rather than force's.

Tightening it quietens a prop dragged along a wall and is much worse on a head, where a
weaker hold cannot keep up with a real hand. Leave it near ten centimetres.

```csharp
public float maxOffset
```

**Returns** [`float`](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.single)

[View source](https://git.cie-group.cz/vr-framework/vrf4/core/-/blob/interaction/physics-hold/Runtime/Scripts/Interaction/PhysicsHold.cs#L129)

### maxOffsetAngle {#maxoffsetangle}

The same bound for rotation, in degrees.

It matters more than it looks, because what it costs is paid at the far end of whatever is
held: on a rod gripped near one end, 45 degrees is a third of a metre of travel at the tip.
Fifteen is the measured knee - looser is springy in two hands and twists the hand about in
one, tighter starts eating real rotation out of a wrist flick.

```csharp
public float maxOffsetAngle
```

### oneHandedStrength {#onehandedstrength}

How much of its strength the hold keeps while the object is held by fewer hands than it wants:
one hand on something marked as needing two, or a steadying hand with nothing positioning.

1 holds it at full strength. The default is well under the point where the hold can keep up
with the hand's own palm, so a rifle held by the foregrip alone lags, swings and is hard to
aim. The object can still be carried, just not used - a feeling rather than a refusal.

```csharp
[Range(0.05, 1)]
```

### resistedSpeed {#resistedspeed}

How much of the written velocity the world has to be taking back, in metres per second, before
the hold counts as resisted and starts bounding itself.

The bounds exist for an object pressed into something. Free, the hold corrects at the gain
and settles in a few steps; resisted, it corrects at the bound and leans rather than
fights. Applying them the whole time leaves a shoved object crawling back into the hand.

```csharp
public float resistedSpeed
```

### slideWhileHeld {#slidewhileheld}

Whether a held object stops rubbing on the world while it is held.

Roll a rod along a table and friction rolls it, turning the grip and the hand with it. A
real hand slides the rod instead, because the grip is stronger than the friction - which is
not something a contact solver can be told directly. Taking the friction away says it in
the language it reads.

Only while held, and only for the held object: whatever it hits keeps its own friction.

```csharp
public bool slideWhileHeld
```

**Returns** [`bool`](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.boolean)

[View source](https://git.cie-group.cz/vr-framework/vrf4/core/-/blob/interaction/physics-hold/Runtime/Scripts/Interaction/PhysicsHold.cs#L157)

### slipSpin {#slipspin}

How hard the world has to be turning a held object, in radians per second, before its grip is
allowed to give at all. Only read when [`maxGripTwist`](/api/vrframework-interaction-runtime/HoldSettings#maxgriptwist) is set.

Most disagreement between hand and object is not the world's doing - an object lags a
turning wrist, and a two-hand hold aims along the line between the grips rather than along
either wrist. This separates "the cube I am pushing caught the table edge and rolled" from
"I turned my wrist and the object took a moment to follow".

```csharp
public float slipSpin
```

**Returns** [`float`](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.single)

### suspendGravity {#suspendgravity}

Turns the object's gravity off while it is held. On, because gravity is otherwise a bias the
write has to spend part of its acceleration budget cancelling every step, and what is left over
shows up as a fixed sag that reads as a weak grip.

```csharp
public bool suspendGravity
```

### turnsTheHand {#turnsthehand}

Whether turning this object turns the hand with it. Off for the stick on a valve: the hand
rides it round but the wrist keeps facing where the player is facing. Nothing about how firmly
the object is held changes, so with nothing else turning it this has no effect at all.

```csharp
[Tooltip("Whether turning this object turns the hand with it.\n\nOn, and it is held as if it were part of the hand: turn your wrist and it turns, and whatever else turns it winds your wrist round too. Right for anything carried, aimed or swung.\n\nOff for the stick on a valve: the valve takes the stick round and the hand goes with it, but the wrist keeps facing where the player is facing rather than being wound round with it.\n\nThis changes nothing about how firmly the object is held, so with nothing else turning the object it does nothing at all.")]
public bool turnsTheHand
```
